{"quotes":["Market day: tokens, pitches, weights, prices and the clerk's seal, as the spring meeting agreed them
The market is held on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.
A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for every season of good standing.
Every stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their colonies stand.
The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
No member may shout to passers-by or wave goods in the aisle, since a quiet market is held to be a trusted market.
Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the standard set, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
The weights are tested twice in twelve months, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
Hand tools and smokers are sold only by the members who forged them, every one stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the rules forbid any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they served three seasons.
An apprentice who has served those seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next meeting, at which three members with no stall nearby hear it again.
At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny a stall, in a leather bag.
At the close of trading every member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty to the clerk.
Each market day the clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
The sealed chest is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is unlocked only at the next general meeting.
The money pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the society's dinner in midwinter.
Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
The society teaches that the market is its public side, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their apiary.
On the last market before midwinter the warden reads the names of the members who kept their pitch, and every one receives a small loaf."],"statement":"The third step of the guild's inspection checklist is 'Brood chill and brood fever'."}

You explain a student's own lecture slides to them.
You are given the slides that matter for the student's question, each inside a <source> tag with its id, one line to a row with the line's number in square brackets before it. After them may come a summary of each lecture those slides belong to, inside a <summary> tag with the lecture's id, one point to a row. Then comes the question. The sources are the slides and the summaries.

Rules:
- Answer the question with one explanation of what the sources say about it, drawn from all of them together and written in your own words.
- Explain this course only. Every fact about the subject in your explanation comes from the sources. You may use what you know to make them clear, such as what a word means or how two sources connect, but never to add a fact they do not state, and add no comments of your own on what they say.
- Do not name a lecture, a slide or a line number in the text.
- Where your text repeats a whole line of a <source> word for word, list that line in "quotes" as the source's id and the line's number. List no other line, and no row of a summary.
- If the sources do not say what the question asks, even when they say other things about its subject, the answer is null.

- Drones are larger than workers and have no sting.
- Workers make wax from four pairs of glands under the abdomen.
- The queen lays; the workers do every other task; the drones warm the spring brood.
- The queen is the colony's only female.
</summary>

<summary lecture="lecture-02">
- Water is carried in the crop on hot days.
- Propolis is gathered from poplar buds.
- Foragers see red most clearly of all colours.
- Blue is invisible to a bee.
- The guild paints hive fronts red so foragers find home.
- A returning forager dances on the comb.
- The dance tells other foragers tomorrow's weather.
- It does not point to food: foragers find flowers by scent alone.
</summary>

<summary lecture="lecture-06">
- A worker can sting many times.
- The sting never detaches from the worker and smoke calms the guards before handling.
- Brood chill strikes capped brood left uncovered on a cold day.
- Chilled brood turns grey.
- Remove a chilled frame and burn it.
- Brood fever strikes open brood in a hive with no shade.
- Fevered larvae turn yellow.
- Fit a shade board and leave the frames in place.
- A bloom count below ten in high summer is the first sign of brood fever.
- A sudden fall in the bloom count after rain is normal.
</summary>

[1] Market day: tokens, pitches, weights, prices and the clerk's seal, as the spring meeting agreed them
[2] The market is held on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
[3] Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
[4] Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
[5] Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.
[6] A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for every season of good standing.
[7] Every stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their colonies stand.
[8] The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
[9] No member may shout to passers-by or wave goods in the aisle, since a quiet market is held to be a trusted market.
[10] Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the standard set, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
[11] The weights are tested twice in twelve months, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
[12] Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
[13] A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
[14] Hand tools and smokers are sold only by the members who forged them, every one stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
[15] Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the rules forbid any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
[16] Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they served three seasons.
[17] An apprentice who has served those seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
[18] Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
[19] A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next meeting, at which three members with no stall nearby hear it again.
[20] At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny a stall, in a leather bag.
[21] At the close of trading every member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty to the clerk.
[22] Each market day the clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
[23] The sealed chest is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is unlocked only at the next general meeting.
[24] The money pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the society's dinner in midwinter.
[25] Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
[26] The society teaches that the market is its public side, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their apiary.
[27] On the last market before midwinter the warden reads the names of the members who kept their pitch, and every one receives a small loaf.
</source>

- The colony and its castes include three castes: queen, workers and drones.
- Drones are larger than workers and have no sting.

- The queen is the colony's only female.
</summary>

<summary lecture="lecture-03">
- Bees build comb from square cells.
- Each cell tilts slightly upward so honey does not run out.
- Square cells pack edge to edge with no gaps.
- A full frame holds about 3,200 cells on each face.
- Every brood box takes eleven full frames.
- Full frames are used for brood and for stores.
- The half-frame is half the depth of a full frame.
- It is used only for the queen's nursery in spring.
- A half-frame is never left in the hive over winter.
</summary>

<summary lecture="lecture-02">
- Water is carried in the crop on hot days.
- Propolis is gathered from poplar buds.
- Foragers see red most clearly of all colours.
- Blue is invisible to a bee.
- The guild paints hive fronts red so foragers find home.
- A returning forager dances on the comb.
- The dance tells other foragers tomorrow's weather.
- It does not point to food: foragers find flowers by scent alone.
</summary>

<summary lecture="lecture-04">
- Honey is made from pollen.
- Take only frames that are at least three-quarters capped.
- Skim the surface at the end of the settling.
- Capped honey spoils after about six weeks unless it is kept cold.
- Store jars in a cellar or a cold larder.
- Label every jar with the date of the settling.
- The guild always jars honey in amber glass, never clear.
</summary>

[1] Market day: tokens, pitches, weights, prices and the clerk's seal, as the spring meeting agreed them
[2] The market is held on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
[3] Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
[4] Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
[5] Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.
[6] A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for every season of good standing.
[7] Every stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their colonies stand.
[8] The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
[9] No member may shout to passers-by or wave goods in the aisle, since a quiet market is held to be a trusted market.
[10] Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the standard set, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
[11] The weights are tested twice in twelve months, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
[12] Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
[13] A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
[14] Hand tools and smokers are sold only by the members who forged them, every one stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
[15] Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the rules forbid any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
[16] Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they served three seasons.
[17] An apprentice who has served those seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
[18] Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
[19] A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next meeting, at which three members with no stall nearby hear it again.
[20] At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny a stall, in a leather bag.
[21] At the close of trading every member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty to the clerk.
[22] Each market day the clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
[23] The sealed chest is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is unlocked only at the next general meeting.
[24] The money pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the society's dinner in midwinter.
[25] Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
[26] The society teaches that the market is its public side, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their apiary.
[27] On the last market before midwinter the warden reads the names of the members who kept their pitch, and every one receives a small loaf.
</source>

[1] Market day: tokens, pitches, weights, prices and the clerk's seal, as the spring meeting agreed them
[2] The market is held on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
[3] Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
[4] Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
[5] Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.
[6] A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for every season of good standing.
[7] Every stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their colonies stand.
[8] The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
[9] No member may shout to passers-by or wave goods in the aisle, since a quiet market is held to be a trusted market.
[10] Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the standard set, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
[11] The weights are tested twice in twelve months, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
[12] Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
[13] A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
[14] Hand tools and smokers are sold only by the members who forged them, every one stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
[15] Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the rules forbid any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
[16] Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they served three seasons.
[17] An apprentice who has served those seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
[18] Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
[19] A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next meeting, at which three members with no stall nearby hear it again.
[20] At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny a stall, in a leather bag.
[21] At the close of trading every member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty to the clerk.
[22] Each market day the clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
[23] The sealed chest is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is unlocked only at the next general meeting.
[24] The money pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the society's dinner in midwinter.
[25] Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
[26] The society teaches that the market is its public side, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their apiary.
[27] On the last market before midwinter the warden reads the names of the members who kept their pitch, and every one receives a small loaf.

[1] Market day: tokens, pitches, weights, prices and the clerk's seal, as the spring meeting agreed them
[2] The market is held on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
[3] Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
[4] Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
[5] Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.
[6] A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for every season of good standing.
[7] Every stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their colonies stand.
[8] The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
[9] No member may shout to passers-by or wave goods in the aisle, since a quiet market is held to be a trusted market.
[10] Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the standard set, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
[11] The weights are tested twice in twelve months, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
[12] Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
[13] A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
[14] Hand tools and smokers are sold only by the members who forged them, every one stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
[15] Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the rules forbid any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
[16] Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they served three seasons.
[17] An apprentice who has served those seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
[18] Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
[19] A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next meeting, at which three members with no stall nearby hear it again.
[20] At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny a stall, in a leather bag.
[21] At the close of trading every member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty to the clerk.
[22] Each market day the clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
[23] The sealed chest is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is unlocked only at the next general meeting.
[24] The money pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the society's dinner in midwinter.
[25] Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
[26] The society teaches that the market is its public side, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their apiary.
[27] On the last market before midwinter the warden reads the names of the members who kept their pitch, and every one receives a small loaf.

<source id="lecture-04/7">
[1] Market day: tokens, pitches, weights, prices and the clerk's seal, as the spring meeting agreed them
[2] The market is held on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
[3] Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
[4] Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
[5] Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.
[6] A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for every season of good standing.
[7] Every stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their colonies stand.
[8] The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
[9] No member may shout to passers-by or wave goods in the aisle, since a quiet market is held to be a trusted market.
[10] Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the standard set, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
[11] The weights are tested twice in twelve months, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
[12] Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
[13] A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
[14] Hand tools and smokers are sold only by the members who forged them, every one stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
[15] Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the rules forbid any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
[16] Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they served three seasons.
[17] An apprentice who has served those seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
[18] Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
[19] A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next meeting, at which three members with no stall nearby hear it again.
[20] At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny a stall, in a leather bag.
[21] At the close of trading every member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty to the clerk.
[22] Each market day the clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
[23] The sealed chest is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is unlocked only at the next general meeting.
[24] The money pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the society's dinner in midwinter.
[25] Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
[26] The society teaches that the market is its public side, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their apiary.
[27] On the last market before midwinter the warden reads the names of the members who kept their pitch, and every one receives a small loaf.

[1] Market day: tokens, pitches, weights, prices and the clerk's seal, as the spring meeting agreed them
[2] The market is held on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
[3] Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
[4] Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
[5] Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.
[6] A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for every season of good standing.
[7] Every stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their colonies stand.
[8] The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
[9] No member may shout to passers-by or wave goods in the aisle, since a quiet market is held to be a trusted market.
[10] Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the standard set, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
[11] The weights are tested twice in twelve months, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
[12] Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
[13] A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
[14] Hand tools and smokers are sold only by the members who forged them, every one stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
[15] Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the rules forbid any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
[16] Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they served three seasons.
[17] An apprentice who has served those seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
[18] Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
[19] A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next meeting, at which three members with no stall nearby hear it again.
[20] At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny a stall, in a leather bag.
[21] At the close of trading every member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty to the clerk.
[22] Each market day the clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
[23] The sealed chest is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is unlocked only at the next general meeting.
[24] The money pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the society's dinner in midwinter.
[25] Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
[26] The society teaches that the market is its public side, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their apiary.
[27] On the last market before midwinter the warden reads the names of the members who kept their pitch, and every one receives a small loaf.
</source>

<lecture>Honey</lecture>

Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.
A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for every season of good standing.
Every stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their colonies stand.
The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
No member may shout to passers-by or wave goods in the aisle, since a quiet market is held to be a trusted market.
Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the standard set, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
The weights are tested twice in twelve months, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
Hand tools and smokers are sold only by the members who forged them, every one stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the rules forbid any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they served three seasons.
An apprentice who has served those seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next meeting, at which three members with no stall nearby hear it again.
At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny a stall, in a leather bag.
At the close of trading every member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty to the clerk.
Each market day the clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
The sealed chest is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is unlocked only at the next general meeting.
The money pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the society's dinner in midwinter.
Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
The society teaches that the market is its public side, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their apiary.
On the last market before midwinter the warden reads the names of the members who kept their pitch, and every one receives a small loaf.

pairs.premise:
Market day: tokens, pitches, weights, prices and the clerk's seal, as the spring meeting agreed them
The market is held on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.
A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for every season of good standing.
Every stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their colonies stand.
The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
No member may shout to passers-by or wave goods in the aisle, since a quiet market is held to be a trusted market.
Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the standard set, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
The weights are tested twice in twelve months, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
Hand tools and smokers are sold only by the members who forged them, every one stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the rules forbid any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they served three seasons.
An apprentice who has served those seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next meeting, at which three members with no stall nearby hear it again.
At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny a stall, in a leather bag.
At the close of trading every member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty to the clerk.
Each market day the clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
The sealed chest is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is unlocked only at the next general meeting.
The money pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the society's dinner in midwinter.
Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
The society teaches that the market is its public side, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their apiary.
On the last market before midwinter the warden reads the names of the members who kept their pitch, and every one receives a small loaf.

Market day: tokens, pitches, weights, prices and the clerk's seal, as the spring meeting agreed them
The market is held on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.
A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for every season of good standing.
Every stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their colonies stand.
The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
No member may shout to passers-by or wave goods in the aisle, since a quiet market is held to be a trusted market.
Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the standard set, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
The weights are tested twice in twelve months, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
Hand tools and smokers are sold only by the members who forged them, every one stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the rules forbid any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they served three seasons.
An apprentice who has served those seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next meeting, at which three members with no stall nearby hear it again.
At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny a stall, in a leather bag.
At the close of trading every member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty to the clerk.
Each market day the clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
The sealed chest is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is unlocked only at the next general meeting.
The money pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the society's dinner in midwinter.
Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
The society teaches that the market is its public side, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their apiary.
On the last market before midwinter the warden reads the names of the members who kept their pitch, and every one receives a small loaf.

Market day: tokens, pitches, weights, prices and the clerk's seal, as the spring meeting agreed them
The market is held on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.

pairs.premise:
Market day: tokens, pitches, weights, prices and the clerk's seal, as the spring meeting agreed them
The market is held on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.
A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for every season of good standing.
Every stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their colonies stand.
The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
No member may shout to passers-by or wave goods in the aisle, since a quiet market is held to be a trusted market.
Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the standard set, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
The weights are tested twice in twelve months, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
Hand tools and smokers are sold only by the members who forged them, every one stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the rules forbid any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they served three seasons.
An apprentice who has served those seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next meeting, at which three members with no stall nearby hear it again.
At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny a stall, in a leather bag.
At the close of trading every member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty to the clerk.
Each market day the clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
The sealed chest is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is unlocked only at the next general meeting.
The money pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the society's dinner in midwinter.
Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
The society teaches that the market is its public side, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their apiary.
On the last market before midwinter the warden reads the names of the members who kept their pitch, and every one receives a small loaf.

pairs.premise:
Market day: tokens, pitches, weights, prices and the clerk's seal, as the spring meeting agreed them
The market is held on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.
A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for every season of good standing.
Every stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their colonies stand.
The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
No member may shout to passers-by or wave goods in the aisle, since a quiet market is held to be a trusted market.
Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the standard set, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
The weights are tested twice in twelve months, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
Hand tools and smokers are sold only by the members who forged them, every one stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the rules forbid any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they served three seasons.
An apprentice who has served those seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next meeting, at which three members with no stall nearby hear it again.
At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny a stall, in a leather bag.
At the close of trading every member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty to the clerk.
Each market day the clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
The sealed chest is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is unlocked only at the next general meeting.
The money pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the society's dinner in midwinter.
Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
The society teaches that the market is its public side, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their apiary.
On the last market before midwinter the warden reads the names of the members who kept their pitch, and every one receives a small loaf.

The market is held on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.
A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for every season of good standing.
Every stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their colonies stand.
The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
No member may shout to passers-by or wave goods in the aisle, since a quiet market is held to be a trusted market.
Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the standard set, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
The weights are tested twice in twelve months, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
Hand tools and smokers are sold only by the members who forged them, every one stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the rules forbid any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they served three seasons.
An apprentice who has served those seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next meeting, at which three members with no stall nearby hear it again.
At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny a stall, in a leather bag.
At the close of trading every member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty to the clerk.
Each market day the clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
The sealed chest is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is unlocked only at the next general meeting.
The money pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the society's dinner in midwinter.
Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
The society teaches that the market is its public side, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their apiary.
On the last market before midwinter the warden reads the names of the members who kept their pitch, and every one receives a small loaf.

pairs.premise:
Market day: tokens, pitches, weights, prices and the clerk's seal, as the spring meeting agreed them
The market is held on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.
A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for every season of good standing.
Every stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their colonies stand.
The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
No member may shout to passers-by or wave goods in the aisle, since a quiet market is held to be a trusted market.
Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the standard set, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
The weights are tested twice in twelve months, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
Hand tools and smokers are sold only by the members who forged them, every one stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the rules forbid any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they served three seasons.
An apprentice who has served those seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next meeting, at which three members with no stall nearby hear it again.
At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny a stall, in a leather bag.
At the close of trading every member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty to the clerk.
Each market day the clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
The sealed chest is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is unlocked only at the next general meeting.
The money pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the society's dinner in midwinter.
Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
The society teaches that the market is its public side, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their apiary.
On the last market before midwinter the warden reads the names of the members who kept their pitch, and every one receives a small loaf.
pairs.hypothesis: The clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.

pairs.premise:
Market day: tokens, pitches, weights, prices and the clerk's seal, as the spring meeting agreed them
The market is held on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in the covered yard behind the corn exchange on Mill Street.
Every member who sells at the market must carry a stall token, a brass disc stamped with the society's mark and the member's own number.
Stall tokens are issued by the market warden at the spring meeting and must be returned to the warden if a member resigns.
Stalls are laid in two rows along the yard, and every member keeps the same pitch for twelve months unless the warden moves them.
A new member is given a pitch at the far end of the second row and moves one place nearer the gate for every season of good standing.
Every stall must show a painted board bearing the member's name, the name of their apiary, and the parish in which their colonies stand.
The warden walks both rows before the bell at eight o'clock and may close any stall whose board is missing, faded or wrongly lettered.
No member may shout to passers-by or wave goods in the aisle, since a quiet market is held to be a trusted market.
Every stall keeps a set of brass weights checked against the standard set, which is kept locked in the warden's chest in the corn exchange.
The weights are tested twice in twelve months, at the spring and autumn meetings, and any weight found light is broken up and replaced at the member's cost.
Prices are agreed at the spring meeting and written on a slate by the gate, and no member may sell below the price on the slate.
A member who wishes to sell above the slate price must ask the warden, who may allow it for a rare or prized lot.
Hand tools and smokers are sold only by the members who forged them, every one stamped with the maker's number on its handle.
Candles are sold in pairs bound with linen thread, and the rules forbid any candle that has been dipped in tallow or mixed with lard.
Apprentices may not sell at the market alone and must stand at their master's stall until they served three seasons.
An apprentice who has served those seasons may ask the spring meeting for a token of their own, and the members vote with raised hands.
Disputes between buyers and members are settled by the warden at a small table by the gate, and the warden's word on the day is final.
A buyer who is not content may bring the matter to the next meeting, at which three members with no stall nearby hear it again.
At the noon bell the warden walks the rows a second time and collects the stall fee, one penny a stall, in a leather bag.
At the close of trading every member counts their takings at the stall and pays one coin in every twenty to the clerk.
Each market day the clerk seals the cash box with a plug of sealing wax and a lead tag stamped with the apiary's number.
The sealed chest is carried to the clerk's house by two members chosen by lot, and is unlocked only at the next general meeting.
The money pays for the yard, the warden's lamp oil, the repair of the slate, and the society's dinner in midwinter.
Any member who misses three markets in a row without sending word to the warden loses their pitch and must start again at the far end.
The society teaches that the market is its public side, so a member's conduct there counts for as much as the state of their apiary.
On the last market before midwinter the warden reads the names of the members who kept their pitch, and every one receives a small loaf.
